name: Mountain Climbers
tierNote: Safety tier C (content.md 5.1: not in the A or B lists); census.json difficulty tier 3.

claims.text: Mountain climbers are a moving plank: from a raised push-up position the feet are brought forward one at a time toward the chest.

quotes.text: Mountain climbers are like a moving plank: You start in a raised push-up position and hop your feet forward, one at a time, toward your chest.

claims.text: Hands go directly under the shoulders with the arms straight.

quotes.text: Start on your hands and knees with your arms straight and hands placed directly under your shoulders.

claims.text: The body forms a straight line from the back of the head to the heels, on hands and toes.

quotes.text: Extend your legs back behind you, supporting your body on your hands and toes. Your body should form a straight line from the back of your head to your heels (like a regular, raised push-up position or plank).

claims.text: Bring one foot toward the chest, then switch legs quickly as if running, without letting the hips hike up.

quotes.text: From here, hop one foot toward your chest, and then quickly switch legs, as if you’re running. Try not to let your hips hike up as you move.

claims.text: Keep the plank position while the legs alternate.

quotes.text: Maintain that plank position as you continue to alternate legs.

claims.text: Shifting the weight backward makes balance harder; keep the shoulders over the wrists and press slightly forward.

quotes.text: Weight shifting backward. Shifting your weight backward can reduce some of the pressure on your arms and core, but it can also make it tougher to maintain balance and stability.
A helpful adjustment here is to keep your shoulders directly over your wrists and imagine pressing slightly forward.

claims.text: Bouncing on the toes can add impact and may make the movement harder to control; glide the knees forward with smooth steps instead.

quotes.text: Bouncing on your toes. Some people find themselves bouncing on their toes as they drive their knees forward. This can add extra impact, especially for beginners, which might make it harder to keep the movement controlled.
To adjust, focus on moving with smooth, intentional steps, almost as if you’re gliding your knees forward rather than bouncing.

claims.text: Some back rounding is natural with fatigue; if it becomes excessive, draw the shoulders down and back and engage the core.

quotes.text: Some rounding in your back is natural, especially as you start to fatigue. If you feel your back rounding excessively, try focusing on drawing your shoulders down and back, which supports a neutral spine position.
Engaging your core helps to keep your torso steady, which can help you feel stronger and less strained throughout the movement.

claims.text: Easier versions: step instead of hopping, put the hands on a sturdy bench or step, or shorten the knee drive.

quotes.text: Step, instead of jump. Rather than jumping to switch legs, step one foot forward, then step it back, and repeat with the other leg.
quotes.where: Mountain Climbers Modifications, To make mountain climbers easier:

quotes.text: Place your hands on an elevated surface, like a sturdy bench or step. This reduces the load on your arms and core, making the exercise less intense than starting from the floor.
quotes.where: Mountain Climbers Modifications, To make mountain climbers easier:

quotes.text: Instead of bringing your knee all the way to your chest, only bring it halfway or as far as is comfortable.
quotes.where: Mountain Climbers Modifications, To make mountain climbers easier:

claims.text: Progression: a faster pace raises the cardio and core demand.

quotes.text: Pick up the pace. Do the movement at a faster pace to increase the cardio intensity. This will also challenge your core and legs to move quickly and efficiently.
quotes.where: Mountain Climbers Modifications, To make mountain climbers harder:

claims.text: You may feel the core, shoulders and arms, and the glutes, thighs and hips working; the hip flexors lift the legs.

quotes.text: As you do each rep, you might feel your core, shoulder, and arm muscles working, as well as your butt, thighs, and hips.
quotes.where: To do mountain climbers, after step 4

quotes.text: Hip flexors. These muscles help you flex at the hip (thus the name) when you walk and do other activities that require lifting your legs.
Rectus abdominis. This sheet of muscle — often called the "six-pack" muscle — spans the front of your abdomen

claims.text: Planks and push-ups load the wrist bent back; in patients with pain on the back of the wrist in this position, MRI found an abnormality in 84 %. This is a patient series, not a risk estimate for healthy exercisers.

quotes.text: Many exercise disciplines incorporate upper extremity weight-bearing exercises in an extended wrist posture, for example push-ups, plank position, and various yoga and Pilates poses.
MRI demonstrated an identifiable dorsal abnormality in 84% of patients with dorsal wrist pain associated with weight bearing on the extended wrist.

claims.text: Programmed by time: beginners 2–3 sets of 15 seconds on, 15 off; intermediate 3–4 sets of 20 on, 20 off; well conditioned 4–5 sets of 30 on, 30 off.

quotes.text: Mountain climbers are usually programmed by time rather than reps. Beginners should start with 2 to 3 sets of 15 seconds of work and 15 seconds of rest, which totals about 1 to 2 minutes.
quotes.where: FAQ: How many mountain climbers should I do?

quotes.text: At intermediate level, use 3 to 4 sets of 20 seconds on and 20 seconds off, and if you are well conditioned, 4 to 5 sets of 30 seconds on and 30 seconds off.
quotes.where: FAQ: How many mountain climbers should I do?

claims.text: For strength, 2–3 sets of 10–15 slow, controlled reps (slow is better for beginners); for HIIT, 6–8 rounds of 20 seconds fast with 10 seconds rest.

quotes.text: As part of an overall program focusing on muscular strength and conditioning, complete 2–3 sets of 10–15 slow and controlled repetitions.
quotes.where: How to do mountain climbers with proper form

quotes.text: As part of a cardiovascular program with a HIIT focus, complete 6–8 rounds of fast mountain climbers for 20 seconds, with a 10-second rest in between.
quotes.where: How to do mountain climbers with proper form

quotes.text: They can also be performed at a slow, controlled tempo, which is better for beginners.

claims.text: Progress by lengthening the interval before adding sets, and end the set as soon as the hips start bouncing rather than pushing to the clock.

quotes.text: Progress by extending the interval before adding sets, and end the set as soon as your hips start bouncing rather than pushing to the clock.
quotes.where: FAQ: How many mountain climbers should I do?

claims.text: Hips coming up too high (a triangle or Downward Dog shape) is a common technique fault of this exercise; one source lists letting the hips pike up first on its common-mistakes list and cues keeping the hips level rather than letting them rise.

quotes.text: As for challenges with technique, it’s common for the hips to come up too high during mountain climbers, creating a triangle or Downward Dog shape.
Letting your hips pike up. If your backside rises toward the ceiling, you have made the plank easier and taken the core out of the exercise. Keep a straight line from head to heels.
Drive one knee in. Lift your right foot off the ground and bring that knee toward your chest, keeping your hips level rather than letting them rise.
quotes.where: How to Do Mountain Climbers, step 3

claims.text: Keep a steady breathing rhythm through the whole interval; one coach says holding the breath is very common on this exercise, and that most women do it the first few times they try this.

quotes.text: Holding your breath. Very common on this one and it kills your endurance. Find a rhythm and keep breathing through the whole interval.
Breathe. Find a consistent breathing rhythm rather than holding your breath, which is what most women do the first few times they try this.
quotes.where: How to Do Mountain Climbers, step 6

claims.text: Set a pace at which the hips stay level and the back flat; going faster than you can hold makes the hips bounce, which one coach says almost every woman she watches does.

quotes.text: Slow down. I know that sounds backwards on an exercise built for speed, but almost every woman I watch do these goes fast enough that her hips start bouncing up and down and the core stops working entirely.
quotes.where: How to Do Mountain Climbers, Julie’s Tip (after step 6)

quotes.text: Set a pace where your hips stay completely level and your back stays flat, then hold that pace for the whole interval.
quotes.where: How to Do Mountain Climbers, Julie’s Tip (after step 6)

quotes.text: Going faster than you can hold. Speed is not the goal, sustained position under speed is. If your hips are bouncing, you are past your pace.

claims.text: Hands drifting forward, out in front of the shoulders, puts far more load on the shoulders; the hands belong directly under the shoulders.

quotes.text: Hands drifting forward. Your hands belong directly under your shoulders. When they creep out in front, your shoulders take on far more load than they should.

claims.text: Letting the hips sag drops the load into the lower back and can arch it; squeeze the glutes and brace before moving the legs.

quotes.text: Letting your hips sag. The opposite problem drops the load into your lower back. Squeeze your glutes and brace before you start moving your legs.
Alternatively, sometimes your hips may drop too low, creating an excessive arch in your lower back.

claims.text: If the wrists bother you, raise the hands on a bench (less weight on the wrists) or hold dumbbells or push-up handles to keep the wrists neutral (less wrist extension).

quotes.text: If your wrists bother you, elevate your hands on a bench or use dumbbells to keep the wrists neutral.
quotes.where: Mountain Climber FAQs, Are mountain climbers safe for women over 40?

quotes.text: This option puts less weight on your wrists and upper body, which is useful if you’re looking to build strength gradually in these areas or need to consider an injury.
quotes.where: Variations on mountain climbers, Incline modification

quotes.text: This decreases the amount of extension in your wrists compared with having your hands flat on the floor. It may feel more comfortable if you experience issues with your fingers or wrists.
quotes.where: Variations on mountain climbers, Pushup handles modification

claims.text: For wrist pain the NHS advises stopping or cutting down the activities that cause it; its examples are not exercise, so applying it to mountain climbers is an inference (R-LB5-2 candidate).

quotes.text: stop or cut down activities that are causing the pain – for example, typing, using vibrating tools for work, or playing an instrument
quotes.where: How you can ease wrist pain yourself, Do

plate.viewWhy: The knee drive toward the chest (c4), the straight head-to-heel line (c3) and the hands-under-shoulders stack (c2, c6) are sagittal; the hip-hike fault reads from the side.
plate.frames: Cycle convention (architecture section 1): one half-cycle, from the high plank to one knee driven toward the chest; Trace follows the driving knee; tempo covers one cycle.
plate.start: High plank on hands and toes, arms straight, hands under the shoulders (c2), straight line from the back of the head to the heels (c3).
plate.end: One knee driven toward the chest, the other leg still straight behind, hips not hiked (c4), shoulders still over the wrists (c6).

checkpoints.label: Hands under shoulders
checkpoints.what: Arms straight, hands directly under the shoulders, shoulders over the wrists.

checkpoints.label: Straight line
checkpoints.what: Head to heels in one line, as in a plank.

checkpoints.label: Knee to chest
checkpoints.what: One foot comes forward toward the chest, then the legs switch.

mistake.what: Hips hike up as the knee drives forward.
mistake.why: The anchor's own how-to step warns against it (c4); it breaks the plank line the movement depends on (c3, c5).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 1: the hips coming up (c16, c4; the head's pick). Step 1 hits for faults of this exercise: Healthline's "As for challenges with technique, it’s common for the hips to come up too high during mountain climbers, creating a triangle or Downward Dog shape." (c16); Julie Lohre's "almost every woman I watch do these goes fast enough that her hips start bouncing up and down" (c18: going too fast, her list item 4 "Going faster than you can hold"), read as a "most people" hit (D-SUP-LB7-DIPREPS); her "Holding your breath. Very common on this one" (list item 5) and "rather than holding your breath, which is what most women do the first few times they try this" (c17), which are not candidates (D-SUP-LB10-BREATH). Several faults pass step 1, so step 2's order decides: no quote ties any of them to harm (Lohre's "you have made the plank easier and taken the core out of the exercise", "the core stops working entirely" and "it kills your endurance", and Healthline's "your head would also hang down too low", are not harm); all are on Lohre's "Common Mistakes to Avoid" list and all are sourced directly; the earliest of them on that list is "Letting your hips pike up" (item 1). The hips coming up stays the top fault. Set aside at step 1: Hinge Health's "Here are a few common adjustments to keep in mind" is a list sentence; "Some people find themselves bouncing on their toes" (c7) and "Some rounding in your back is natural" (c8) use "some"; "Many people believe that exercises like mountain climbers need to be done in a specific way to avoid injury" is a belief about exercise and names no fault; "often called the "six-pack" muscle" is a name. Lohre's "Mountain climbers are usually programmed by time rather than reps" (c13) is programming; "This is usually what gives out first on longer intervals" and "the upper body often fatigues first on longer intervals" are about muscles; "This is where I start most women who cannot yet keep their hips level on the floor" says where she starts a modification, not how often the fault happens; "For most women, yes" and "a solid finisher for most women" are about safety and programming. Healthline's "Mountain climbers are usually performed at a fast pace" is about use, and "sometimes your hips may drop too low" (c20) uses "sometimes". Nance's "Occult dorsal ganglion cysts were the most common sources of pathology (76%)" is about scan findings, not a fault. Harm quotes about faults that did not pass step 1 (not reached): Hinge Health's bouncing on the toes "This can add extra impact" (c7) and gliding that "minimizes strain on your ankles"; "Engaging your core helps to keep your torso steady, which can help you feel stronger and less strained throughout the movement." (c8, back rounding); Lohre's sagging hips "drops the load into your lower back" (c20) and hands drifting forward "your shoulders take on far more load than they should" (c19). Hinge Health's weight shifting backward (c6) states no harm. The side view shows the hips raised above the head-to-heel line, a still sign, so drawable stays true. Pick and drawable unchanged (pilot A plate; D-SUP-LB8-PILOTS). Fetcher scan (2026-10-22), further hits set aside: Hinge Health's list heading is "‘Mistakes’ when practicing mountain climbers" (bouncing on the toes, weight shifting backward, rounding the back); it names none of the step-1 faults, so it does not change step 2's order. Hinge Health's "This movement engages many major muscle groups" and "They’re some of the most powerful muscles in your back" are about muscles; "Everyone is different, which is why you may need to modify this exercise" names no fault; "Shifting your weight backward can reduce some of the pressure on your arms and core" (c6) is a lower load, not harm; "Mountain climbers are a functional movement that may reduce the risk of falls and injury.", "taking some of the strain off of your muscles and joints", "Reduces back pain." and "strengthening your core can help lessen back pain" are benefits; its physical-therapy and liability lines name no fault. Lohre's "They are one of the most efficient conditioning moves" is about the exercise; her "Watch For" cell "Hips piking up or sagging" is a label, not a frequency word. Healthline's "works many muscles", "can be modified to many levels" and "they may reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease" name no fault; "need to consider an injury" (c21) is about a modification; "It’s best to use an exercise mat to avoid slipping" is equipment. Nance's "Many exercise disciplines incorporate upper extremity weight-bearing exercises" is about exercise in general, and its pain lines describe patients, with no fault. The NHS wrist page's frequency and pain lines ("There are many causes of wrist pain.", "Wrist pain is often caused by bruising or injuring your wrist" and its symptom lists) are about wrist pain in general, with no fault of this exercise; its stop line is c22. Reading applied: frequency words count only in a sentence about this exercise's own fault (Healthline's hips, Lohre's pace and breath lines), list sentences and statements about muscles, programming, benefits or all exercise are set aside, and the step-1 tie is broken by Lohre's list order.

tells.text: Hips stay level as legs switch

tempo.text: Default (beginner): 2-3 sets of 15 s on, 15 s off (c13), switching legs quickly, as if running (c4); slow and controlled suits beginners (c14). Progressions: 20 s on/20 s off, then 30 s on/30 s off, lengthening the interval before adding sets; end the set when the hips start bouncing (c13, c15). High-intensity option only: 6-8 rounds of 20 s fast, 10 s rest (c14). No source gives steps per second.

grip.wrist: Wrist bent back under body weight (as in planks and push-ups, c12).
grip.note: No source found on finger spread or weight through the heel of the hand.

setup.step: Start on hands and knees, arms straight, hands under your shoulders.
Step your legs back onto your toes; body in one straight line.
Bring one foot toward your chest, then switch legs quickly.
Keep the plank position the whole time.

posture.point: Straight line from head to heels.

handlingMistakes.fix: Keep your hips level; slow down.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Weight shifts back toward the feet.
handlingMistakes.fix: Shoulders over wrists, press slightly forward.
Glide the knees forward with smooth steps.

rows.means: You might feel these muscles working.
The hip flexors lifting the legs.

rows.where: Pain on the back of the wrist
rows.fix: Stop the exercise. Hands on a bench, or dumbbells to keep the wrists neutral.
rows.fixNote: The shared wrist box covers what to do next. The bench and dumbbell option is c21's: Healthline says the bench option "puts less weight on your wrists", and Lohre says "If your wrists bother you, elevate your hands on a bench or use dumbbells to keep the wrists neutral."

risks.risk: Pain on the back of the wrist in the loaded, bent-back position.
Bouncing on your toes can add impact and make control harder.

zooms.right: Palm flat, hand directly under the shoulder.
zooms.wrong: Hands ahead of the shoulders, weight shifted back.

zooms.right: Hips level with the head-to-heel line.
zooms.wrong: Hips hiked up as the knee drives.

libraryDiff.why: Library: core primary; hip_flexors and abs secondary. Hinge Health lists hip flexors and rectus abdominis among the muscles worked (c11), which matches. It also lists chest, deltoids, triceps, glutes and quads, but it is a coaching list with no EMG, so no change is proposed.

anchorNote: Hinge Health (physical therapists) mountain climbers page read in full. No ACE, NSCA or ACSM mountain climber page was reachable, and PubMed has no technique or EMG study of the exercise (search 2026-09-30: 3 hits for mountain climber AND EMG, none relevant).
unsourced: Cadence (steps per second); work and rest times are now sourced (c13, c14).
Finger spread and weight through the heel of the hand (palm-flat archetype).
Where the driving foot lands (toe tap vs floating).
